facts.fact_text: The applicant's co-workers expressed a wish to hold a public assembly on Constitution Day on 12 December 2009.
The applicant, in his capacity as trade union leader, decided to help his co-workers hold a public assembly on Constitution Day on 12 December 2009.
According to the applicant, his help to his co-workers was 'an indirect expression of his own opinion'.
The applicant distributed banners to his co-workers.
The applicant explained to his co-workers that it would be more practicable to stage solo demonstrations.

To avoid prosecution for holding a public assembly without notifying the authorities in advance, the applicant suggested that his co-workers position themselves at some distance from each other, for instance on different streets.
At the time of the events on 12 December 2009, there was no federal or regional statutory requirement concerning the minimum distance between simultaneous solo demonstrations.
The applicant was arrested.
The applicant was taken to the police station after his arrest.
The applicant was held at the police station for three hours.
On 18 December 2009, a justice of the peace found the applicant guilty under Article 20.2 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
The justice of the peace fined the applicant 1,500 Russian roubles (approximately 35 euros at the time).
On 22 January 2010, the Surgut Town Court upheld the judgment of the justice of the peace of 18 December 2009.
At the time of the events on 12 December 2009, there was no federal or regional statutory requirement concerning the minimum distance between simultaneous solo demonstrations.
The justice of the peace found that it was incumbent on the applicant to lodge a prior notification about the event to the competent authority as required by section 7 of the Public Events Act.

In his appeal, the applicant noted that the Public Events Act defined a 'picket' as a form of public expression of opinion where one or more citizens with placards, banners and other means of visual expression stationed themselves near the target object of the 'picket'.
In his appeal, the applicant argued that there had been a separate 'target object' for each solo demonstrator.
In his appeal, the applicant argued that the demonstrators had been positioned at a considerable distance from each other, for instance thirty metres apart for two of them.

A summary of domestic law and practice concerning regulations relating to public events in Russia is contained in Novikova and Others v. Russia, application nos. 25501/07, 57569/11, 80153/12, 5790/13 and 35015/13, §§ 47-85, judgment of 26 April 2016.

On 18 December 2009, a justice of the peace found the applicant guilty under Article 20.2 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
The justice of the peace fined the applicant 1,500 Russian roubles (approximately 35 euros at the time).
The justice of the peace considered that the applicant and his co-workers had met in one place.
The justice of the peace considered that the applicant had given instructions to his co-workers.
The justice of the peace considered that the applicant had distributed banners to his co-workers.
The justice of the peace considered that the applicant had taken his co-workers to the place of the demonstration.
The justice of the peace found that the above circumstances disclosed the presence of a group event in the form of a static demonstration (a 'picket').
The justice of the peace found that the above circumstances confirmed the applicant's role as organiser of the group event.
The justice of the peace found that it was incumbent on the applicant to lodge a prior notification about the event to the competent authority as required by section 7 of the Public Events Act.

In his appeal, the applicant noted that the Public Events Act defined a 'picket' as a form of public expression of opinion where one or more citizens with placards, banners and other means of visual expression stationed themselves near the target object of the 'picket'.
In his appeal, the applicant argued that there had been a separate 'target object' for each solo demonstrator.
In his appeal, the applicant argued that the demonstrators had been positioned at a considerable distance from each other, for instance thirty metres apart for two of them.
In his appeal, the applicant argued that he could not be lawfully considered as an organiser of a group event.
On 22 January 2010, the Surgut Town Court upheld the judgment of the justice of the peace of 18 December 2009.
